analysis.title: People, Power And Politics: Morgan Stanley Maps The Three Ways AI's $1.6 Trillion Capex Plan Can Collapse
key_insights: Morgan Stanley public policy strategist Ariana Salvatore frames the main constraints on the AI infrastructure buildout as people, power and politics. The bank still expects the buildout to happen, as a conditional buildout.

MS does not expect a federal pause because of the national-security framing and a likely presidential veto of restrictive legislation. It sees the midterms laying groundwork for potential legislation in 2029.

The binding levers are local: interconnection, large-load rate design, siting, permitting and tax abatements are decided at the state level, so governors and utility commissions matter more than Senate races.

MS sees AI sentiment as most constructive under a Republican sweep, broadly neutral under divided government and least constructive under a Democratic sweep, because non-incumbent candidates tend to propose tougher restrictions.
JPMorgan's Democrat Factor is up 20% as the market prices a Democratic sweep, which is the scenario MS calls least constructive for AI sentiment, with about two weeks to the November 3 election.
The data center debate has moved from whether to restrict to how: pause outright or proceed subject to conditions. Tax breaks are the consensus target regardless of who wins.

Utility commissions may matter most because they decide dockets on cost allocation and generation approval, which are legally durable. Georgia's 3-2 GOP PSC majority flips if Democrats win both seats. A Louisiana vote on about $15B of Entergy gas units for Meta's Richland Parish expansion lands near the election.

States flagged by MS hold almost 60 GW of data centers under construction, planned or on acquired land (Texas 24 GW, Pennsylvania 11 GW), versus MS's forecast of 32 GW of compute capacity added by hyperscalers and neoclouds in 2027.

Texas Governor Abbott paused new approvals in early August pending an audit of about 250-300 projects and ordered a halt to new data centers in September. ERCOT faces 474 GW of interconnection requests, 90% data centers, against an all-time peak demand record of 91.1 GW on July 22, 2026.
MS sees the entire US short about 80-100 GW through 2030, a deficit of about 100 nuclear power plants.

Ohio's leading governor candidates, Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, both want new data center restrictions. Acton backs a conditional moratorium. Ramaswamy's pledge requires free electricity for nearby residents and no tax abatements.
Only 7% of voters rank data centers as a top issue, but electricity bills make that enough to matter in close races.

Industry mitigation: hyperscalers signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, Google committed to return more water than its data centers use by 2030, Amazon disclosed global data center water use, and Meta launched a $1B community fund. The House passed a bill making data centers cover their own energy costs.
MS's base case is a conditional buildout: the $1.6T still gets spent, but some of it costs more and lands later, and only in regions where mitigation works.

Second risk is volume and price falling together. Scarcity drives fear of missing procurement, buyers pay up and suppliers stack margins. When capacity catches up, forward-buying reverses and pricing power collapses while suppliers hold high-cost inventory.

MS's analog is the late-2022 memory downturn, when NAND shipments fell about 5% but prices fell 20-30%. Even a plateau in hyperscaler capex could leave volumes resilient while pricing and upstream margins fall. MS says the risk of both falling at once is underappreciated.

Amazon attributed most of its 2026 capex increase to rising memory costs with no change to its build plan, so part of the capex growth is price, and memory is where it would unwind first. Global smartphone shipments fell 22% amid the memory crisis.
Power is the most tangible risk per MS. Its Powering AI model shows a 32 GW net US shortfall through 2028 (34% of the 97 GW needed) after time-to-power solutions, and about 72 GW through 2029.

Chain exposure: most exposed are components bought ahead of need that ship with the rack (memory, networking, optical, ODM servers), with memory most sensitive. Electrical, cooling and construction equipment face slower backlog conversion. Relative winners are behind-the-meter generation (gas turbines, eventually modular nuclear), fuel cells and powered shell providers.
MS expects hyperscalers to build more capex outside the US if domestic power stays tight.
PJM scrapped its emergency data center power auction earlier in October after a FERC rebuke. BlackRock's Larry Fink warned last week that a data center ban would put the US in recession.

The author adds a fourth risk, paying for it: MS credit strategists show 2027 as the year free cash flow hits its deepest hole and lower-rated borrowers run out of cushion. November 3 is the first test.

tension_points.bull_case: MS stays constructive on the buildout: industry mitigation (Ratepayer Protection Pledge, water commitments, community funds) supports a conditional buildout, the power gap delays rather than destroys demand, and long-term agreements can manage the price cycle.
tension_points.bear_case: The three risks feed each other: politics slows interconnection and siting, widening the power gap and stranding chips bought at peak prices, so volumes and prices fall together as in the 2022 memory downturn.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Democratic sweep in the November 3 midterms and utility commission flips such as Georgia's PSC would signal tighter restrictions and weaker AI sentiment.
